# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is a careful follow-up. It does most of what the earlier critiques asked for:
- a registered mediation test, with mediators specified before the 24-month outcomes were known;
- a second, independent hours measure;
- a like-for-like comparison over time;
- an honest description of the Halden subset as survivors.

Its answers to the re-analysis and the meta-analysis are mostly fair. Its finding that the meta-analysis's four long follow-ups were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours confirms that the "no decay" claim was unsupported.

The arithmetic checks out:
- Output per hour: 0.966/0.88 gives +9.8% on timesheets, and 0.966/0.89 gives +8.5% on logs.
- Halden subset: 96.8/86.6 gives +11.8%.
- Counter arm: 12% more staff is consistent with the nine-month figures (0.83 × 1.067 = 0.886, and 1/0.886 ≈ 1.13). A 9% rise in cost per contact is plausible if about a quarter of costs are not staff costs.

There are still several problems. One may change how the main result should be read.

## 1. The size of the decline is overstated, and part of it may come from the control group

**Mixed measures.** The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% … to 8.5%". That compares a timesheet figure with a log-based one. The like-for-like change is **12.5% → 9.8%**, which the main text correctly uses. The Summary should match it.

**Not statistically established.** The 9- and 24-month intervals overlap heavily: +6.9 to +18.4 against +4.6 to +15.2. "Has therefore declined" is stronger than the data support. The text's own wording, "consistent with some fading", is the right register.

**Control-group contamination.** In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their meetings, and their output per hour rose about 4.1%. That improves the control group by roughly 2/7 × 4.1 ≈ 1.2 percentage points. The measured gap at 24 months shrinks accordingly. That could account for close to half of the 2.7-point decline.

So some of the apparent fading may be the control group catching up, not the treatment wearing off. The paper reports the meeting audit but doesn't connect it to the decline. The fix is to report the 24-month estimate both with and without those two offices, or to adjust for the timing of the audit.

## 2. Meetings may explain most of the gain, not 47%, but it depends on what the logs measure

A simple accounting check, using the paper's figures and assuming meeting time sits inside timesheet hours:

| | Timesheet hours, pre → 24m | Meeting hours | Non-meeting hours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Treated | ~37.9 → ~33.4 | 7.4 → 3.9 | ~30.5 → ~29.5 (−3%) |
| Control | ~37.9 → ~37.9 | 7.2 → 7.0 | ~30.7 → ~30.9 (+1%) |

Treated non-meeting hours fell about 4% relative to control, and output per employee fell 3.4%. Output per *non-meeting* hour is therefore roughly unchanged, about +0.5%.

On this rough accounting, almost the whole per-hour gain is accounted for by time moved from meetings to case work. The registered model attributes only 47% to meetings. The two can differ legitimately, because the mediation model estimates something different from simple accounting. But a gap this large should be explained.

**What "active log-in time" captures is ambiguous.** It is described as recording "time staff are working on cases":
- **If it excludes meetings,** treated log hours should have fallen only about 4%, given the meeting cuts, not 11%. The figures would then be inconsistent.
- **If it includes meetings** (staff logged in during them), it is a total-time measure rather than "working on cases", and the description should say so.

The paper needs to state which it is.

**Source of the baseline meeting figures.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. This report gives baselines of 7.4 and 7.2 hours, presumably taken from calendar history after the fact. That is fine if so, but it should be stated, and the extraction method should match the one used at month 24.

## 3. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result

- **No randomisation of mediators.** Meeting cuts and fatigue weren't randomly assigned. Mediation shares rely on the assumption of no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which the Limitations section acknowledges. The Summary's "confirms" doesn't fit that caveat. "Is consistent with" or "supports" would.
- **Office-months are not independent.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds little information. The effective sample is 14 offices, with repeated, correlated months. Intervals as tight as 28–66% need either small-cluster methods or an account of how clustering was handled. Neither is described.
- **Selective credit.** The report is right that the registered test answers the "post hoc story" objection about where the hypothesis came from. But it doesn't settle the causal question.

## 4. The finding changes what the debate is about, and the paper partly recognises this

If the per-hour gain comes mostly from removing meetings, it is real: it isn't a measurement artifact. But it may not require cutting hours. The control offices' meeting audit points that way, though only weakly: two offices, a before–after comparison, and possible seasonality and regression to the mean.

The paper handles this well, noting that no arm reorganised without cutting hours. It should give the point more prominence. For employers, "cut meetings" and "cut hours to force meeting cuts" are different recommendations, with very different costs. A trial arm that reorganises without cutting hours is the obvious next study.

## 5. Problems raised at nine months that are still unaddressed

- **Small-cluster inference.** With 7 offices per arm, conventional clustered standard errors are too small. The paper still doesn't say whether it used a wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference. The claim that the interval "excludes zero by a clear margin" (lower bound +3.4%) depends on this.
- **Sick days.** The −27% may still be partly mechanical if staff now work four days instead of five, since a week of illness then counts as fewer sick days. The rota pattern and an hours-based absence measure are still missing.
- **Backlog and deadlines.** The nine-month Limitations section raised the risk of backlogs growing past statutory deadlines. At 24 months, the case system can answer that directly. Data on backlog size, case age and deadline compliance aren't reported.
- **Cost per case.** Cost is reported for the counter arm (+9% per contact) but not for case processing. There, staff kept full pay and claimed overtime.
- **Quality.** Appeal overturn rates (3.2% v 3.0%) are still given as levels, with no interval or difference-in-differences estimate.

## 6. Retention may be part of the unexplained 35%

Treated offices lost staff at about half the control rate (4.1% v 7.9% a year). Over two years, they keep more experienced caseworkers, and experienced caseworkers are generally faster. This is a genuine effect of the policy, but it is a different mechanism from rest or meetings. Staff tenure could be tested as a mediator.

## 7. The Halden subset

- **"Upper bound" isn't justified.** There is no comparison group, and the baseline is more than two years old. Changes over that period, such as new tools, economic shifts or client mix, could push the estimate in either direction. "Likely optimistic" is defensible; "upper bound" is not.
- **Survivors three times over, not twice.** These organisations completed the pilot and continued it, as the paper says. They also submitted records and agreed to follow-up: 14 of the 23 that had records. The nine that declined may differ.
- **The reversion that doesn't fit.** The marketing agency reverted because of client deadlines. Under the meta-analysis's coding, marketing counts as discretionary work, not coverage-bound. The Summary's phrase "client-facing or coverage obligations" smooths over this. Work driven by external deadlines that the organisation doesn't control may be a third category, distinct from both backlog work and work requiring presence.

## 8. The responses to earlier papers

- **The re-analysis.** The response is fair and appropriately targeted. The measurement critiques are accepted, and the "entirely an artifact" conclusion is refuted by a design that meets the re-analysis's own standards. The month-ten extrapolation of self-reported energy is also clearly contradicted.
- **The meta-analysis.** The response is correct, and it relies on information the meta-analysis should have reported in its main text. One qualification: "declined by about a quarter" (12.5 → 9.8 is a 22% decline) should come with the caveats from point 1. The decline isn't statistically established, and part of it may come from the control group.

## Overall

**Well supported:** in case processing, a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% persists at two years on strict measures. Output per employee is slightly below control. In counter work, the scheme failed on service and cost. Meeting reduction is a substantial part of the mechanism.

**Needs revising:**
- The Summary's mixed-measure "12.5% → 8.5%" and its "confirms".
- Treatment of the control offices' meeting audit, as both contamination and a possible cause of the apparent decline.
- What log time measures.
- Small-cluster inference.
- Backlog and cost data for case processing.

The most consequential open question is now whether the gain needs the hours cut at all. That needs an arm that reorganises work without reducing hours.

If useful, I can put together a synthesis of where the evidence stands across all five documents, or a referee report on this one.
